name: Special situations credit investing
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Forced Selling in Corporate Bonds
caseLead: Stressed corporate bonds can trade below their likely recovery value when rating changes, refinancings or corporate transactions force investors to sell. The opportunity persists because many bond funds and insurers must follow rating and index rules regardless of price, while sanctions, trade restrictions and changes in monetary policy keep creating new stressed issuers.
caseRest: The main risk is that the issuer's financial position worsens and bond recoveries fall short of expectations. Losses can also arrive together because forced selling spreads across many bonds in a market sell-off, as in December 2008 and March 2020. The estimated 9.4% annual return therefore comes with 8.8% volatility, an 18.0% worst fall and negative return skew, so a run of recoveries can hide the size of the loss in a stressed year.
figNote: Each card shows the highest level of the US high yield credit spread during the episode, which is the extra yield investors demand over Treasuries to hold lower-rated corporate bonds. The spread has averaged about 5% over the long run, while readings above 8% signal severe stress in the corporate bond market.

events.title: Forced selling drives credit spreads to a record
events.text: After Lehman Brothers failed, investors sold corporate bonds to meet redemptions, and the high yield spread reached a record 22% in December 2008. The strategy lost because bond prices fell far below recoverable value before markets stabilised.

events.title: Oil price slump creates energy bond opportunities
events.text: OPEC's decision to keep producing took oil below $30 a barrel and pushed the high yield spread to 9% in February 2016. The strategy gained because bonds of producers with strong balance sheets were priced for default, and spreads narrowed in the following months.

events.title: Trade tensions and rate rises widen spreads
events.text: US-China trade tensions and Federal Reserve rate rises led investors to sell high yield bonds in December 2018, lifting the spread to 5%. The strategy lost because forced sales by funds facing outflows pushed bond prices below estimated recovery values.

events.title: Fed support narrows spreads after a sharp widening
events.text: The Covid sell-off lifted the high yield spread to 11% in March 2020, before the Federal Reserve announced support for corporate bond markets. Results were mixed because the strategy lost in the first weeks and then gained as forced sellers stopped and spreads narrowed.

events.title: Credit Suisse rescue writes off bank capital bonds
events.text: Swiss authorities arranged UBS's takeover of Credit Suisse in March 2023 and wrote off about $17bn of its bank capital bonds, widening spreads on similar issues. Results were mixed because the write-off hurt holders of those bonds, while senior and secured credits recovered quickly.

events.title: Tariff announcement briefly widens credit spreads
events.text: The April 2025 US tariff announcement lifted the high yield spread to about 5% as investors reduced risk. The strategy gained because spreads narrowed within weeks, so bonds bought at the widest levels recovered.

instrument: US and European corporate bonds, including stressed and recently downgraded issues; held three to twelve months; priced daily
rules: Bonds bought when forced selling or index rules push the price well below estimated recovery value; positions held through the refinancing, spin-off or rating change; exposure limited by issuer and sector
costs: Estimated bid-ask spreads, which are wide for stressed bonds, and commissions deducted at each trade
constructionTitle: Strategy construction, from forced sellers to credit protection

legs.position: Long stressed bonds near recovery value
legs.purpose: Earns recovery as forced selling ends
Buys from holders forced to sell by rating rules

legs.position: Protection on the high yield index
legs.purpose: Hedges a broad rise in credit spreads
Provides collateral and funds new purchases

entry: Price at least 8 points below estimated recovery value
size: Single issuer capped at 3%; each sector capped at 15%
exit: Position closed at 90% of estimated recovery value, or after 12 months
stop: Position closed if the issuer's recovery estimate is cut by 20%
marketWatch: High yield spreads, the volume of bonds recently downgraded and the schedule of debt that matures in the next year are the main indicators because they show where forced selling is most likely. Rating agency decisions, sanctions and central bank policy matter most when they change borrowers' access to refinancing.

favourable.heading: Forced sellers leave the market
favourable.text: The end of forced selling favours the strategy because bonds then return towards their recovery value. After the Federal Reserve announced support for corporate bond markets in March 2020, spreads narrowed sharply within weeks.

favourable.heading: Refinancing markets stay open
favourable.text: Open refinancing markets favour the strategy because stressed issuers can repay maturing debt instead of defaulting. After the oil price recovery in 2016, energy producers with sound balance sheets raised new funds and their bonds rose.

favourable.heading: Rating rules create temporary mispricing
favourable.text: Rules that force funds to sell downgraded bonds favour the strategy because the sales push prices below the value that issuers are likely to repay. In 2020, bonds of companies downgraded from investment grade to high yield recovered much of their loss within months.

adverse.heading: Defaults exceed estimates
adverse.text: A rise in defaults hurts the strategy because recovery values fall below estimates and bonds trade down towards them. In 2015 and 2016, many energy producers defaulted as oil prices fell below $30 a barrel.

adverse.heading: Forced selling lasts longer than expected
adverse.text: Prolonged forced selling hurts the strategy because bonds bought at a discount fall further before buyers return. After Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, the high yield spread rose to 22% in December and bonds fell below recovery estimates.

adverse.heading: Liquidity disappears in a sell-off
adverse.text: A loss of trading liquidity hurts the strategy because bid-ask spreads widen and positions cannot be reduced at fair prices. In March 2020, many corporate bonds could be sold only at large discounts until the Federal Reserve intervened.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's estimated peak-to-trough change in value during each event, using bond prices adjusted for estimated recovery values and the cost of trading stressed bonds. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in credit spreads, interest rates and default rates by sector, which are then applied to the strategy's current bond holdings and credit protection.
